name: Monarchism
summary: Monarchism advocates monarchy, rule or headship of state by a hereditary king. The sources that name it and can be tied to it here are the counter-revolutionary writer Joseph de Maistre, who treats the Revolution as an antireligious crime crowned by regicide, and the Action Française tradition of Charles Maurras. It is mainly a doctrine about the form of the state and says little on economic or most social questions.

keyFigures.role: Counter-revolutionary writer on throne and altar
keyFigures.quote: De Maistre was painted as a fanatical monarchist

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Bossuet (Book IX) lists arms among the necessary supports of royalty and treats the prince's wars and armies as part of his duties.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Hereditary rank in the throne is the heart of the doctrine: Bossuet (Book II) and Maurras (Discours préliminaire) hold that the crown must pass by birth, which the statement would abolish.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Maistre, Essai (s29), sections I and XLV: a constitution is a divine work and not the product of the living, and reform of institutions belongs to men only with terrible restrictions, so the present generation does not decide which institutions to keep.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Bossuet (Book I, Art. 4) says the authority of the laws does not depend on the consent and acquiescence of the people, and rests the king's authority on God.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Maistre's Préface (axioms 1 and 12) and Considérations ch. VI say no constitution results from deliberation and that no assembly of men can constitute a nation.

decide-locally.rationale: Maurras, Enquête sur la monarchie (s25), Discours préliminaire X: decentralisation to the province, town and village ('un pouvoir de vie autonome') is called an indispensable part of the reform, though the king remains the federating head.

democracy-best.rationale: Maurras (Discours préliminaire) calls the belief that democracy is legitimate in France an error and prefers the hereditary crown, and Maistre's Préface prefers hereditary monarchy to every other government.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Maurras (Discours préliminaire) rejects choosing the sovereign by popular election, plebiscite or competition in favour of the hereditary crown, and Maistre's Préface calls the elective headship the worst government.

direct-votes.rationale: Maurras, Enquête sur la monarchie (s25), Discours préliminaire IX: the 'culte des majorités souveraines' is attacked; majority success is a fact of force, so laws are not to be settled by popular vote.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Bossuet (Book III) has princes act as God's ministers, Maistre (Considérations ch. VI; Essai Préface) has constitutions and legislators act under God, and Maurras (Discours préliminaire) holds all authority rests on a transcendent source.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Maurras's Discours préliminaire (III) makes hereditary succession from male to male by primogeniture the core of monarchy; Bossuet (Book II, 9th proposition) calls hereditary monarchy the best and Maistre's Préface calls it the most stable and natural government.

elective-rulers.rationale: Maistre's Préface calls elective monarchy the worst form of government, and Maurras (Discours préliminaire) holds that election of the head of state makes the supreme office a prize for money and foreign interests, which the hereditary crown avoids.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Maurras, Enquête sur la monarchie (s25), Discours préliminaire, the passage on 'empirisme organisateur': in place of celebrating equality, 'even before the law', attention goes to natural differences; elsewhere the dream of the equality of men is called 'mauvais'.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Bossuet (Book IV, Art. 1 and Book IX) shows the prince as captain-general of the people with the sword and the army as supports of royalty.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: The League presents it as part of constitutional monarchy that Parliament is dissolved in the sovereign's name and that the royal prerogative remains as a safeguard if normal democratic processes break down.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: Bossuet, Politics (s30), Book IX, on war and its just motives (7th proposition, p. 290): lists as just motives for war unjust hostility, refusal of passage on equitable terms and violation of ambassadors, which is force initiated beyond self-defence.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Bossuet's work is drawn from the very words of Scripture, and in Book I and Book VIII he grounds the laws and the prince's justice in the divine law.

leader-cult.rationale: The League holds that the sovereign as head of state embodies all Canada and all Canadians and urges honouring the monarch publicly (pictures, anthem, naming places), so honouring a national figure as the embodiment of the nation is acceptable.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The League's case for the Crown defends a sovereign as head of state separate from the head of government, whose functions are normally formalities, and treats the monarchy as the central pillar of parliamentary democracy.

morality-needs-religion.rationale: Bossuet (Book VII, Art. 1, and Book VIII, Art. 1) holds that religion and justice are the constitutive principles of states and that justice is founded on religion.

more-religion-public.rationale: Bossuet (Book VII) makes the prince's first duty the protection of religion as the good of nations, and Maistre (Considérations ch. VI) finds the strength of French monarchy in its theocratic element.

national-church-status.rationale: Bossuet (Book VII, Art. 5, 9th proposition) says the prince should use his authority to destroy false religions in his state, and Maistre (Considérations ch. VIII) praises the theocratic element of the French monarchy with its bishops in civil government.

natural-rulers.rationale: Maurras (Discours préliminaire) denies that governing capacity is a quality of the royal blood and says a mediocre hereditary sovereign still serves, so fitness to rule does not rest on innate aptitude.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Maurras (Discours préliminaire) holds that the hereditary crown removes the supreme office from party divisions and gives the nation a single centre above competition.

organic-representation.rationale: Maurras, Enquête sur la monarchie (s25), Discours préliminaire X: representation should rest on 'les représentations des intérêts locaux et professionnels, fédérées et confédérées' ('au peuple dans ses États'), not on elected party politics.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Maurras (Discours préliminaire) makes the monarchy antiparliamentary and strong enough to break the encroachments of parliamentarism, and Bossuet (Book IV) holds legitimate command belongs to the prince alone.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Bossuet, Politics (s30), Book VII, 9th and 10th propositions on the prince's duties: the prince may use strictness in matters of religion, and to allow blasphemy and atheism would leave the gravest crimes the least punished.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Bossuet (Book VI, Art. 2, 5th proposition) holds that even open impiety and persecution do not free subjects from obedience and that nothing justifies active resistance to the sovereign.

restore-past-order.rationale: Maurras (Discours) wants the old institutions destroyed by the Revolution restored, and Maistre (Considérations ch. X) defends the return to monarchy.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Maistre (Considérations ch. V) treats the Revolution as a satanic, antireligious crime, and Bossuet (Book VI) allows subjects no active resistance.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Bossuet's Book III, Art. 1 states that royal authority is sacred and that the person of kings is sacred, as ministers of God anointed with a sacred unction.

separate-church-state.rationale: Bossuet (Book VII) names religion and justice as the constitutive principles of the state, and Maistre (Considérations ch. V) condemns the Revolution's decree that the nation pays for no worship.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Maistre, Essai sur le principe générateur (s29), sections XLIV-XLV: reformation belongs to man only 'in a secondary way and with a host of terrible restrictions', and he shares the 'aversion of all good minds for innovations'; Bossuet, Politics (s30), Book I on the laws, holds it dangerous to change established laws without necessity.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Bossuet (Book IV, Art. 1, 3rd and 4th propositions) says there is no coercive force against the prince and he is exempt from the penalties of the laws, though bound by their directive force.

state-harmful.rationale: Bossuet (Book I, Art. 3) says a government is necessary to form nations, and Maurras (Discours) wants a strong state restored.

strong-leader.rationale: Maurras (Discours, Les réponses) says the monarchy must be strong and will break the encroachments of parliamentarism; Bossuet (Book IV, Art. 1) says without absolute authority the prince can neither do good nor suppress evil.

taxation-theft.rationale: Bossuet, Politics (s30), Book X, article 1 on finances and taxes (6th and 7th propositions): the people's contribution to public expenses is their own preservation, since what they give up secures the rest, though the prince must moderate it.

total-state.rationale: Maurras (Discours, Les réponses) wants the state strong in its own domain and the citizen free in his, with decentralisation and freedom of association as conditions of civil liberty.

traditional-family.rationale: Bossuet, Politics (s30), Book II: the first empire among men is the paternal one, the model of cities and of the whole of human society; Maurras, Enquête sur la monarchie (s25), Discours préliminaire: the families now in dissolution are to be rebuilt as part of the restored institutions.

scope: Monarchism is the advocacy of monarchy: rule or headship of state by a hereditary king. The defining sources split it into strands, and this audit covers them as the sources tie them to the name: (1) the counter-revolutionary, throne-and-altar monarchism of Joseph de Maistre, whom New World Encyclopedia says was 'painted as a fanatical monarchist' (s18); (2) the integral-nationalist monarchism of Charles Maurras and Action Française, the founder of Action Française, an 'ardent monarchist' who sought a restoration of the monarchy as the one institution able to unify society (s19, s33), which McClelland calls 'Maurras's way of being radical' as a reactionary (s31); (3) the early-modern absolutist theory of monarchy (Bossuet, Filmer), the subject of the Cuttica and Burgess volume 'Monarchism and Absolutism in Early Modern Europe' (s32); and (4) modern constitutional monarchism, for which the Monarchist League of Canada's own account presents the Crown as the central pillar of parliamentary democracy (s34). Where these strands disagree (absolute versus constitutional monarchy) the audit records a split. Bossuet's and Maistre's own texts count as key works or key figures' texts only as far as these sources tie them to monarchism.
